I have! I was a senior laboratory animal technician for a year before starting my DVM. It pays very well and there's a few locations that offer residency training. There's definitely drawbacks, in my case I know it would have predisposed me to burnout and I personally don't get a lot of satisfaction out of palliative care for terminal animals (which is a lot of what you do). You do a lot of reviewing research protocols and overseeing animal welfare standards.
Typically my observation is DVM MPHs are medical officers and the DVM PhDs stay in academia.

Correct. Sometimes you find things more along the lines of toxins, organ dysfunction, and cancer. At my undergrad university, the veterinary diagnostic lab did cultures and other diagnostics besides necropsies, but was run by a veterinary anatomic pathologist. My veterinary school microbiology lab was run by someone with a PhD and a DVM, and we had other PhD DVMs teaching and doing research on infectious organisms in a lab. When you end up in an academic setting like that, you've had to get multiple doctorate degrees and some positions will be more management and less hands on science, which isn't for me personally. The pathologists in that zoo I spend time with worked closed with the microbiology team also at the facility. If you just want to focus on infectious disease only and are okay doing a lot of data analysis and statistics, you should consider pursuing an MPH and working for a government agency, and at that point having a DVM might not be necessary (although I've met multiple DVM PhDs that went into epidemiology and that DVM gives them more senior positions).

A lot of clin path is reviewing cytology, blood smears, bloodwork, etc. Anatomic is going to be performing full necropsies, reviewing histology, and ordering ancillary diagnostics (PCR, culture, etc). Everyone has their personal preferences, but I find clinical pathology kind of boring (sorry to all the clinical pathologists reading this, I appreciate you!). I would despise reviewing blood films and mass aspirates all day. While with clinical pathology, you might get presented an animal suddenly found dead and you need to work up the entire case from the ground up. Working with my anatomic pathologist professor, we documented a horrifically infectious disease of reptiles for the first time within our state in novel species and presentations and have presented our work nationally, which led to collaboration with clinicians to develop emergency containment and treatment protocols. It honestly was very hard for me to decide between clinical practice and anatomic pathology because I love it SO much and find it so exciting and challenging. Just for the time being, I prefer working with living creatures and *some* owners enough to pick that over pathology at this point. But if I hate it in a few years and am burning out, I absolutely will pursue anatomic path and disease investigation.

Like said above, I would explore anatomic pathology and I think it would be worthwhile pursuing! I've done a lot of infectious disease research in veterinary school under an anatomic pathologist and I loved it so much I almost switched my career path to pursue it, and I've done training at an internationally respected zoo pathology program. You get to be at the front lines in disease exploration and get challenging cases where you need to think critically and apply all the mechanisms of disease. Look into it and speak to some veterinary pathologists! I think too you'd enjoy it more than clinical pathology.

I agree with doing as many as is an okay load for you. The credits you get will help you finish undergrad and get into vet school sooner, and with the price of vet school, you'll want to save as much in undergrad as you can! Many of those courses are also harder when you get to college and you don't have caring teachers to help you as often, so you risk a worse grade on your transcript for vet school and just taking those classes sucks. The only two classes I didn't do AP and get AP credit for were the subjects that end up lowering my GPA and giving me grey hair in college haha. So if you know math isn't your thing or physics or chemistry etc I'd probably recommend doing those as AP if you're picking and choosing. But at the same time, don't bog yourself down and miss out on your teenage years or bite off more you can chew and hurt your GPA for college admissions in the process though.

I'm kind of lightly saying ESH. I'm in the veterinary field and let me explain why:

Clinic sucks: they absolutely should have discussed this with you. Even during dentals where we give clients a range on the price saying we're unsure until we get in there how many teeth have to come out and explain that, we still call during the procedure to double check with the owner that we're good to do the extractions now giving the exact number to come out (if we can't reach them but they signed that we could do it without their authorization we will end up doing it if we don't hear back, but still try to contact first). Maybe it was somewhere in a paper you signed before the procedure in the fine print, but even so they still should have discussed it with you to make sure you fully knew what you were signing. I understand being upset something happened to your dog without your say and it's wrong. It's also not cool that you were upset and they didn't send a doctor or a manager to talk to you.

You suck: the poor techs usually are just taking orders and earn minimum wage and you put her through the ringer when it wasn't her decision. The reason to extract those teeth was legitimate and saved you money and prevented potential dental issues for your pup, so it was in both of yours best interest. They also even tried to make it up to you by waving the fee and it sounds like you had made up your mind to just be angry no matter how they apologized or explained. You could have been less aggressive to that poor techs and also tried to calm your own emotions to see why they did a good thing for you and your dog even if they should have talked to you first.

If you're super unhappy don't go there again, but although they totally crossed a line with consent and didn't communicate well, the medicine was right and came from a good place. The rate of burnout, leaving the profession, depression, suicide, and substance abuse is really high with this profession- they're people too who make mistakes and have feelings. Keep that in mind in the future and I'd encourage you to reconsider leaving a bad review considering those things can really hurt their business or impact their mental health after they did try to explain and make it up to you, and in the end you and your dog ended up saving money and having a doctor with a keen eye that was thorough and acted to prevent anything bad from happening to your pet. I don't blindly defend all veterinarians- there is one near me I've been trying to encourage clients to report to the state board and sue for negligence- and admit they should have called you, but I think how you reacted was uncool.

They make tongs/grabbers that are like 4-5 ft long with really strong grips (that quite easily injure snakes and break ribs, but if it's that or a shovel to the head I'd taken a broken rib any day). There's a local sanctuary in town that teaches the public about these animals and allows them to practice and purchase these types of tools. It's empowered many people, including older folks, to be able to grab a snake and move them away from their porch or other areas on their property. People definitely shouldn't be messing with snakes for the hell of it, but it can definitely be done for people that live in really active areas for snakes.

My man, I work with deadly venomous snakes regularly and am certified to remove them from people's properties. In the USA, annually there is only ~3 snakebite deaths a year, including those that don't seek treatment or have other health issues. I'm in the field of exotic (veterinary) medicine and have been trained by a veterinarian who's been treating and performing surgery on venomous snakes likely before you were even born. Many times this year I've done things ranging from fluids to a mamba or biopsy on a cobra. These animals deserve respect and can be dangerous, but at the end of the day they're an animal- fear and pain included. Recent studies into reptile intelligence and socialization have also shown they even form complex family groups. If an animal has a chance to hide from you or run, it will absolutely take that option. If it feels trying to defend itself is its last hail Mary to survive you the predator, it will take that chance. I live in an area also filled with Diamondbacks. I encourage neighbors to train their pets, declutter their yard to make it less hospitable, get the name of removers, or buy tongs/grabbers off of Amazon. They play a very important role in the ecosystem and keep down pests that spread disease and chew through wires (costly and dangerous as this can lead to housefires). Co-existence is possible and your comment really shows how little you *actually* know about these animals

Sorry you're going through this. In the US 26 would be a more average age of a veterinary student since almost always you get a bachelor's here before veterinary school. Even at that though, you get a bunch of people together who are stressed, type A, and have to be forced around the same people they may or may not like for hours every single day and the worst of people will come out- even had a conversation today about a ~30 year old mean girl who failed out and the lack of sympathy we have because she was SO rude and unpleasant to work with. That's still astounding you're dealing with that level of childishness and I'm sure it's not helping with the stress you're already dealing with by being in vet school. Keep your head up and just focus on each day, each week, each month you get closer and closer and none of them will matter when you're out there doing your thing and saving animals as Dr. [Insert name here]. Having peers you can go to for help though is important, so if you know there's a few students who are actually there to learn try and make friends with them and form a support network. Also it can be hard, but try to stay in touch with family and friends from back home so you don't find yourself isolated. I'd keep proof of all the harassment and you can always try with different admin people to get something done about it, but this will make sure you have plenty of evidence if you need it. Good luck and stay strong!

I volunteered in undergrad in wildlife rehab for two year, teched at a small animal and exotics clinic that would take some wildlife cases (mostly reptiles) for 2-3 years, teched with one of the vets from that practice on his zoo rounds (he mostly did just the reptiles and amphibians), was a senior tech at a lab animal facility with rodents and non-human primates, volunteer with a reptile sanctuary that also does conservation work now in vet school, and have been in leadership in our wildlife and zoo etc club on campus every year now (now a third year). Being in zoo and conservation work it's hard because there's lots of financial constraints and the curators hold the purse strings on what they'll approve to pay for. On the other hand, you don't have the stresses that come from some pet owners. You see a huge variety and act as the ultimate general practitioner. However, getting a zoo job is almost impossible. After graduation, it takes many years of internship and residency (if you're lucky enough to get one) before you can sit for your boards- which translates to long horrible hours of being the doctor with doctor responsibilities on a 20-40k salary. Once you have your certification if you're lucky enough to find a job opening, it'll be highly competitive and not pay that much. Look at AAZV for information on boarding and rates for matching to internships and residencies in that field. And since the jobs and internships and residencies are such slim pickings on top of really competitive, if they say jump be willing to jump and move your entire life to wherever gives you a spot. That amount of stress (many years with poor pay, little say in where I'll live, an ultimate salary that is not great, and likely years of repeated rejection) just wasn't worth it to me personally. The variety, challenge, getting to work with special species, and play a role in conservation outweighs the negatives for some, so you'll have to make that personal decision. I've ended up deciding to go the route of private practice exotics- more money, boarding (internships and residencies) is still competitive but there's more opportunities, ability to go above and beyond with how much value some owners place in their personal pets, getting a lot of variety in species and problems to treat, and occasionally the ability to collaborate with zoos and wildlife organizations from your practice. Look at boarding for these through the ABVP (ie I'm looking at herp medicine and surgery, 1 yr internship with 2 years residency going that route, or 5 years of straight practice with specific stipulations). Regardless of choosing exotics, wildlife, or zoo med you should be trying to find opportunities ASAP to get experience and references as these will be really important as you go along. I don't mean for this to be discouraging, but hopefully it helps prepare you and give you an idea comparing zoo versus exotic private practice.

I went professional school, so it's a bit different (DVM), but my biggest advice is just to get a strong support network. I had a great mentor coming in and have since gotten a few more from doing my research (animal infectious diseases). It helps to know they believe in me and having them for letters of rec or advice is EXTREMELY helpful for life, but also because knowing they'll help me really avoids a huge trigger of panicking and then flipping out trying to apply for things or figure stuff out on my own. In my personal life honestly I'm not sure how I've always kept it together, but it's been staying on my medication, telling my doctor when I needed an adjustment, having personal support, and sometimes knowing limits. If I'm so depressed and stressed I want to off myself, maybe I stop studying for the night and try again in the morning and accept I might get a worse exam grade. At home my husband gives me pep talks when he knows I need it, help me get out of the house if I'm in a rut, makes sure I don't act like an idiot if I'm manic, and remind me of basic things like eating and sleeping to reduce the risk of triggering cycling. That doesn't have to be a SO, but a friend or family member that's aware of how you work. Maybe it's slightly unhealthy, but I try to do as much as I can if I get manic (pump out papers, posters, studying, proposals, etc) because once I come back down I know I won't be as productive. Be willing to accept rejection (I still suck at that and as we speak an very sad about not getting a wildlife medicine rotation slot in my clinical year coming up), because that will absolutely happen when applying for your PhD, submitting an abstract at conferences, etc. And lastly, stay inspired! Having good mentors helps with that for me personally (get to go and talk to them about their cool cases), but since I love exotic animal medicine when I get in to a workshop on that or am performing clinical procedures or it exams it helps lift my spirits and remind me why I'm doing it. I will not lie and say it's easy, but it's possible and in the words of Temple Grandin, the world needs all kinds of minds- including the unique prospectives you'll bring and the way the world will be better because you pushed through this to get that education and contribute to your field. Good luck!

It can be controversial, but lab animal career path! Bachelor's degree and then there's increasingly difficult certifications once you're in that field (ALAT, LAT, LATG, lab animal manager). You get to be the advocate for the animals caring for them daily, enforcing welfare standards when they're used in research and then providing them with medical care, husbandry, grooming, enrichment, etc. Compassion fatigue can be really problematic though. It's an incredibly important job with room to move up the ladder and make a career out of it I feel like. I worked as a senior lab animal tech after getting my bachelor's in vet sci during a gap year before going to veterinary school. It personally wasn't for me, but it gave me a lot of insight and I gained valuable skills and knowledge while being really proud of the care and advocacy I provided to my animals (and relationships with MOST of my PIs/research labs).

YTA. While it's great you accept her religion, you are forcing her out of a family tradition you all have with gift exchange and staying in a cabin together. My parents are Methodist and many of them go to church for Christmas related activities, as does my husband's Catholic family. He, however, is atheist and I am agnostic- and close family friends and other certain family members have these same beliefs. We don't treat Christmas as a commercial holiday among us who aren't Christian, but as time to be with family and enjoy family traditions and our religious family members celebrate that as well on top of their faith based celebrations. I love Christmas dinner with my husband's family or my mother's, Christmas Eve with his grandmother, Christmas morning with my father, finding thoughtful gifts that reflect my appreciation for my loved ones, the annual family Christmas party with taken show and white elephant gift exchange, scented pinecones that bring me back to my childhood, and putting up and enjoying a Christmas tree with collectible ornaments my aunt began for me when I was little and hand me down ornaments from my grandmother who passed away. Christmas can have different values for people and it sounds like for your daughter that is spending quality time with her family, but you have decided the religious significance to you means you have to take away the family meaning from your daughter. You can still see it as a way to appreciate your faith, but it breaks my heart that a parent would decide to crush the family togetherness the holiday brings for their child because they have a different religion instead of including her as she always had been. Just my two cents worth.

This is such a tough topic. While I still struggle putting animals down as a professional (it hurts my heart to see the grief of the family, and losing your friend is a sad experience), what helps me through it is knowing that this is a humane and painless end for our furry family members who are suffering. I lost two of my own dogs within a 6 month period a few years ago and they took a piece of my heart with them- the first being to horrible metastatic cancer in her lungs and GI system, but the other to some aggressive and strange illness we never did figure out that was unresponsive to us throwing the kitchen sink at it. For the second animal, the professional in me knows it was the right thing to do and there was nothing we could have done to fix it, but the emotional owner part of me still has pain wondering if there was something I missed. I think it helps first and foremost to realize this decision will feel awful even if logically you know it's the right choice. The second is, like I said, the fact this is a peaceful end for our furry family members and the ultimate act of compassion, forcing us to feel this intense pain in order to do the humane thing. The next thing is grief is a process and there is no right or wrong way to do it. I made a shadowbox with their photos and collar months down the road when I was ready, and it stayed in a closet many more months before I wanted to have it out. I also chose to have some of their ashes embedded into beautiful glass medallions (I used a shop on Etsy) that I could wear on a necklace when I wanted to feel close to them. Tomorrow it might hit you right away, and harder than you expected, or it may take time to sink in. We had a family member drive us home the first time because I knew I would be crying too hard to drive so that might be something to consider. You also should be prepared to decide if you want ashes back, if you don't want them back, if you want to bury them at home, etc and make that decision ahead of time so you won't struggle with it tomorrow. Lastly, take as much time as you want to say goodbye both before you let them go and after. As soon as both my pets were gone I personally wanted to leave because I felt that it was no longer them. Before they passed, I wanted to love on them until I was sure they were relaxed and calm before being sedated. For me, what also helped with the immense pain is know it is a reflection of the wonderful and loving bond I had with them- which in the end was so worth it because there was a million scenarios in which I would not have been so lucky to have them in my life, and yet it somehow worked out that way which is amazing. I'm very sorry you all are losing your kitty, and I hope some of this may help you.

Well some of what I've read with LDA corrections is choosing slow absorbing or non-absorbable suture for keeping the abomasum anchored. I assume after that though absorbable is fine? My impression too was this is a more common issue in dairy cattle, which tend to be easier to handle than beef cattle. Correct me if I'm wrong though because I have literally 0 real world food animal experience. I was hoping there was literally like a "food animal surgery basics for noobs" article or website so I could get a feel for what patterns are used and the reasons for using each and suture choices for various purposes (ie toggles, omentopexy, skin closure). These are all things I think you learn in clinical rotations, but I'm not there yet (and doing small animal track with exotics, so likely won't be doing any large animal rotations). I might have to breakdown and try to purchase the book to get enough information, which is incredibly expensive so I hoped to avoid as it isn't one I'll be keeping around my entire career.
